newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CFTC loses court ruling on forex trading.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CFTC loses court ruling on forex trading.

text.p: The U.S. Ninth Circuit Court this week affirmed a lower court ruling limiting the jurisdiction of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission over foreign currency transactions.

The ruling affirmed a 1995 lower court decision that the CFTC could not prosecute Frankwell Bullion Ltd under the Commodity Exchange Act for off-exchange sales of positions in foreign currencies to the general public.
Federal circuit courts have taken conflicting positions on the issue, which arises from a 1974 law known as the Treasury Amendment, but the Supreme Court is hearing a case this term.
CFTC officials declined to comment. "The CFTC is studying the ruling," spokesman Dennis Holden said. "We have no comment."

Under the Treasury Amendment, interbank foreign exchange trading is exempt from the jurisdiction of the CFTC. The commission has pursued a narrow reading of the exemption in enforcement cases involving foreign exchange trading.

The Treasury Department has generally favored a broader reading of the exemption. The two agencies have been in talks for months, trying to draft a compromise administrative rule or legislative proposal.

Senator Richard Lugar, chairman of the Senate Agriculture Committee, said he would propose legislation to address the ambiguity next year. One proposal was introduced in the House of Representatives this year and is expected to be revived next year.

In this week's ruling, the court held that Frankwell, a Hong Kong corporation established in 1987, was not a "board of trade" within the meaning of the Treasury Amendment and therefore was covered by the amendment's exemption from CFTC oversight.
"We hold that Congress intended the 'transaction conducted on a board of trade' to mean on-exchange trades," the court wrote.

Limiting the amendment to "only transactions between banks and other sophisticated investors would require this court to craft, without any support from the statutory language, some distinction between sophisticated investors and the general public," the court said in rejecting the CFTC's arguments.
"We hold, as the legislative history indicates, that Congress intended the Treasury Amendment to exempt all off-exchange transactions in foreign currency."

The case before the Supreme Court, William Dunn v. CFTC, revolves around a different phrase in the Treasury Amendment. The court will decide whether the amendment's exemption for "transactions in foreign currency" includes trading options on foreign currency.

The Ninth Circuit also upheld the lower court's ruling that the CFTC should pay 75 percent of receivership fees of $223,242 incurred under a temporary restraining order against Frankwell in June 1994. A month later, the lower court denied the CFTC's request for a preliminary injunction and dissolved the receivership. --Aaron Pressman, 202-898-8312
